disclaimers.short: Not legal, tax, insurance, investment, or financial advice. See the full notice on page 2.
disclaimers.full:
**Important: please read.** Spouse Ledger is a personal record-keeping and organizing tool. It is not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, investment, or financial advice, and using it does not create an attorney-client, accountant-client, or advisory relationship. Laws, deadlines, and institutional rules vary by state and change over time.
Writing a wish or instruction in this book does not make it legally binding or give anyone authority over an account, asset, or business. That generally requires properly executed legal documents (such as a will, trust, power of attorney, or beneficiary designation) and the cooperation of the institution involved.
Before making decisions about estates, trusts, guardianship, beneficiaries, taxes, insurance claims, investments or retirement accounts, or the sale, transfer, or wind-down of a business, consult licensed professionals: an attorney, a CPA or tax professional, an insurance agent, and, where relevant, a financial advisor or business broker.
Spouse Ledger and its creators make no guarantee that the information recorded here is accurate, complete, or current, and assume no liability for decisions made in reliance on it. Keep this book secure, and do not record passwords, full account numbers, or recovery phrases in it.
disclaimers.exit_plan: **Disclaimer:** This section records your plans and where things are. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice. Before deciding anything about selling, transferring, valuing, or winding down the business, including acting on a buy-sell agreement, key-person insurance, an operating agreement, or a broker's or buyer's offer, consult a licensed business attorney and, where relevant, a CPA and a qualified business broker. Do not sign anything from a prospective buyer or broker until your own attorney has reviewed it.
disclaimers.estate: **Disclaimer:** Recording where your estate documents are, and what you want, does not replace having them properly drafted and signed. Wills, trusts, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and guardian nominations must follow your state's legal requirements to be valid. Wishes written in this book, including funeral wishes and the letter, are generally not legally binding. Ask your estate attorney to confirm that your documents, beneficiary designations, and account titling all agree.
disclaimers.insurance: **Disclaimer:** Policy terms, exclusions, and claim deadlines are set by each insurer's contract, not by this worksheet. Beneficiary designations on file with the carrier generally control who is paid, regardless of what a will says. Confirm coverage, premiums, and beneficiaries with your agent or carrier.
disclaimers.tax: **Disclaimer:** Tax rules, deadlines, and penalties vary by jurisdiction and change often. Unpaid payroll taxes can create personal liability. Confirm every obligation and due date with your CPA or tax professional, and call them before changing, skipping, or catching up on any filing or payment.
disclaimers.investments: **Disclaimer:** This worksheet records where assets are. It does not recommend any investment or action. Account ownership, beneficiary designations, and each custodian's rules determine who can access an asset and what steps are required. Digital assets such as cryptocurrency may be permanently unrecoverable without the keys or recovery phrases. Store those securely, never in this book.

items.text: Breathe. Almost nothing on this list has to be decided this week. Don't rush any big decision.
Turn to **Section 14 (First 30 Days)** and work through it in order.
Call the people in **Section 1**, starting with the attorney and the CPA.
Check what cash is available and what bills hit in the next 30 days (**Sections 2 and 6**).
Do NOT cancel insurance, licenses, utilities, or subscriptions until you've checked with the attorney or CPA.
Do NOT make promises to employees, crews, or clients yet.

blocks.text:
**Part 1: The Business** (Sections 1-5): contacts, money, operations, people, and the exit plan.
**Part 2: Home & Family** (Sections 6-13): household money, insurance, legal documents, taxes, investments, property, family, and digital life.
**Section 14**: the First 30 Days checklist and a personal letter.

Fill in what you can. Leave a blank rather than guess, because an honest gap is safer than wrong information. For accounts, write the institution and the **last 4 digits only**. **Never write full account numbers or passwords in this book.** Those belong in your password manager and the sealed emergency envelope (Section 13). Pages that say "where it lives" want a location, such as a drawer, a folder, or an app, not the document itself.

sections.title: Digital Life & Secure Access
sections.subtitle: Write WHERE things are. Never write actual passwords or recovery phrases on these pages.

blocks.text: **Recommended:** use a password manager with emergency access (1Password or Bitwarden). Set an emergency passcode your spouse knows, write it on paper, and seal it in an envelope stored where your spouse will find it. A phone passcode, an authenticator app, and a primary email can each lock someone out of everything else, so cover them first.

blocks.label: Password Manager Used & Emergency Access Set Up?
Where the Sealed Emergency Envelope Is Kept
blocks.helper: Should contain the emergency passcode and master-account recovery info

blocks.label: Phone & Device Unlock
blocks.helper: Who knows my phone passcode? Does my spouse have it? Other devices: laptop, tablet, home computer

blocks.label: Two-Factor Authentication: Where Codes Come From
blocks.helper: Authenticator app on my phone, texts to my number, hardware key. Where backup / recovery codes are stored

blocks.label: Primary Email Accounts
blocks.helper: Personal and business. Most resets go through these, so my spouse needs a path in

blocks.label: Cell Phone Carrier Account
blocks.helper: Whose name, account PIN location, can my spouse manage the lines? The number is also used for 2FA texts

blocks.label: Cloud Storage, Photos, Documents
blocks.helper: iCloud / Google / Dropbox: which account, whose, where family photos are backed up

blocks.label: Online Accounts Index (names only)
blocks.helper: Banks, utilities, government portals (IRS, SSA, state), payroll, merchant services, supplier portals, insurance portals

blocks.label: Social Media & Business Pages
blocks.helper: Facebook business page, Google Business Profile, Instagram, YouTube: who is the admin, who else has access

blocks.label: Website, Domain, Business Email Hosting
blocks.helper: Registrar, host, renewal dates, who has the admin login

blocks.label: Digital Executor / Who Should Handle My Accounts
blocks.helper: Who is trusted to close, memorialize, or take over accounts

sections.title: First 30 Days Checklist
sections.subtitle: Work through this in order. Check each box as you go. Ask the attorney before acting on anything legal or financial.

items.text: Lean on the people in Section 1 and Section 12. Accept help.
Contact the funeral home or arrangements contact. Ask them how many certified death certificates to order; many offices need originals.
Call the attorney (Section 1) and find the will / trust (Section 8).
Call the CPA and bookkeeper. Review cash and the next 30 days of payroll and bills.
Call the insurance agent. Ask about life, key-person, health continuation, and anything with a claim deadline.
Locate the sealed emergency envelope (Section 13) and get into the password manager.
Tell key employees and crew leads calmly: jobs and paychecks will continue. Keep it short, and don't promise anything long-term.
File life insurance claims. Ask each carrier what they need.
Notify Social Security (the funeral home often does this) and any pension or annuity providers.
Contact the mortgage servicer and other lenders. Ask about next steps and don't skip payments.
Visit the banks with death certificates. Ask what is frozen and what is available (Section 6).
Make sure autopay is working for essential bills: utilities, mortgage, insurance, payroll, taxes.
Review Section 5 with the attorney before any decision on the business.
Notify the three credit bureaus to flag the account and prevent identity theft.
Update titles, beneficiaries, and account ownership with the attorney's guidance.
Handle phones, email, and subscriptions. Close or take over accounts after confirming nothing is needed (Section 13).
Tell the school, the pediatrician, and the childcare providers what has changed.
Schedule time with the CPA to cover quarterly tax payments and payroll tax filings.
Make a plan for the business with the attorney and the person in Section 4: keep, sell, or wind down.
Give yourself permission to rest. Nothing here has to be perfect.
